newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco tobacco suit dismissed.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco tobacco suit dismissed.

text.p: A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit filed by the City and County of San Francisco and 10 other California counties against the tobacco industry, according to court papers made public Thursday.
Although the judge dismissed the suit, he ruled that the plaintiffs' lawyers could refile an amended complaint by March 31.

"The lawsuit is still alive," said Elizabeth Laporte, San Francisco's deputy city attorney. "The judge said that we succeeded in pleading most of the elements that we needed to ... and he held that tobacco companies are not immune from suits for fraud under California law."
Laporte added that parts of the ruling would bolster a similar lawsuit filed by the municipalities in state court against the tobacco companies.

The tobacco industry hailed the ruling as a victory in its fight against lawsuits seeking to force cigarette companies to repay states and municipalities for health care costs of smokers. It is believed to be the first ruling to dismiss a lawsuit of this type.

"This decision drives a stake through the heart of this type of lawsuit," said Daniel Webb, an outside lawyer for Philip Morris Cos. Inc. "I think it will be precedent setting and have a wide ranging impact," said Webb, a Chicago lawyer and former U.S. Attorney there.
However, plaintiffs lawyers said they did not see the ruling as a drawback since the judge explained how he wanted the complaint changed and is allowing them to refile.

"The court sustained our primary theories of liability ... we see this as a victory," said Robert Nelson of the San Francisco firm of Lieff, Cabraser, Heimann & Bernstein. "He provided a roadmap of how to proceed and we are willing and able to amend in the way he suggested."
The ruling, dated Wednesday, was issued by U.S. District Judge D. Lowell Jensen in the U.S. District Court in the Northern District of California in Oakland.
San Francisco and the other counties are among a growing number of municipalities and states that have sued the tobacco industry to recoup Medicaid costs.
The attorneys general from 22 states have filed such suits. The first of the trials, which stems from a case brought by Mississippi, is scheduled for June.

The aim of the California suit is to recoup health care costs of smokers. The plaintiffs alleged that the tobacco companies engaged in a racketeering conspiracy to mislead plaintiffs and their residents about the harms of smoking and the addictive nature of nicotine.

Webb said the ruling was particularly important because Jensen wrote that for the plaintiffs to recover money spent on health care for individual smokers, they would have to prove that each of those injuries were actually caused by smoking.
Jensen also found that the racketeering claims should be dismissed because of the remote nature of the plaintiffs' injuries.

The industry argued that the U.S. Supreme Court has held that for racketeering claims to be sustained there has to be a direct relationship between the plaintiffs' injuries and the defendants' alleged conduct. It said that a plaintiff complaining of harm flowing from the misfortunes of a third person was too remote to recover.
Jensen found that the suit failed to meet the proximate cause requirement under the federal racketeering statute.

"First, and most importantly under the present circumstances, it would be extremely difficult for the court to ascertain the amount of damages attributable to defendants' conduct, as there are many other factors that could affect plaintiff's smoking-related damages," he said.
